subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which deficiency disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C in the diet?
questions.explain: A lack of vitamin C prevents proper formation of connective tissue, causing scurvy.

questions.q: Iron is needed in the diet mainly for the formation of which substance?
questions.explain: Iron is a component of haemoglobin, the pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.

questions.q: Why is dietary fibre (roughage) an important part of a balanced diet?
options: It provides bulk that helps the gut push food along by peristalsis
It is digested to release large amounts of energy
It is absorbed to build new body proteins
It kills harmful bacteria in the stomach
questions.explain: Fibre adds bulk to the gut contents, stimulating peristalsis and preventing constipation.

questions.q: A patient is constantly tired and pale, and a blood test shows a low red blood cell count. Which nutrient is most likely missing from their diet?
questions.explain: A shortage of iron reduces haemoglobin production, causing anaemia with tiredness and pale skin.

questions.q: In which organ is bile produced?
questions.explain: Bile is made in the liver and then stored in the gall bladder before release.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the path of food through the alimentary canal?
options: Mouth to oesophagus to stomach to small intestine to large intestine to anus
Mouth to stomach to oesophagus to large intestine to small intestine to anus
Mouth to oesophagus to small intestine to stomach to large intestine to anus
Mouth to stomach to small intestine to oesophagus to large intestine to anus
questions.explain: Food passes from the mouth down the oesophagus to the stomach, then the small and large intestines, before egestion at the anus.

questions.q: The removal of undigested material, such as fibre, from the body as faeces is called:
questions.explain: Egestion is the passing out of undigested food that was never absorbed into the blood.

questions.q: What is meant by assimilation?
options: The movement of absorbed food molecules into cells where they are used
The breakdown of large food molecules into smaller ones
The uptake of digested food from the gut into the blood
The taking of food into the mouth
questions.explain: Assimilation is the use of absorbed nutrients by body cells for processes such as growth and respiration.

questions.q: Which type of tooth is chisel-shaped and used mainly for biting and cutting food?
questions.explain: Incisors at the front of the mouth have sharp, chisel-shaped edges for cutting food.

questions.q: Why are the canine teeth pointed?
options: To grip and tear food such as meat
To grind food into a paste
To cut food into thin slices
questions.explain: The sharp, pointed canines are adapted for holding and tearing food.

questions.q: Bile emulsifies fats in the small intestine. What does this achieve?
options: It breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing the surface area for lipase
It chemically digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol
It neutralises the enzymes that would otherwise digest fat
It absorbs the fats directly into the blood
questions.explain: Emulsification is physical, not chemical, breaking fat into small droplets so lipase can act faster on a larger surface area.

questions.q: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces before it is swallowed. How does this help chemical digestion?
options: It increases the surface area of the food for enzymes to act on
It raises the temperature of the food to speed up reactions
It changes the pH of the food to suit the enzymes
It absorbs water from the food to concentrate it
questions.explain: Smaller pieces have a greater surface area, so digestive enzymes can break the food down more quickly.

questions.q: The enzyme amylase digests starch into which product?
questions.explain: Amylase breaks down starch into the sugar maltose.

questions.q: The enzyme lipase digests fats (lipids) into which products?
questions.explain: Lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.q: Proteases are enzymes that digest proteins into which smaller molecules?
questions.explain: Proteases break the large protein molecules down into amino acids, which can be absorbed.

questions.q: What is the role of the hydrochloric acid produced by the stomach?
options: To kill bacteria in food and provide the acidic pH needed for stomach protease
To emulsify fats before lipase acts on them
To neutralise acid coming from the small intestine
questions.explain: The acid destroys many bacteria in food and gives the low pH at which the stomach's protease works best.

questions.q: A food sample is mixed with amylase at 37 degrees C. After ten minutes, adding iodine solution gives a brown colour instead of blue-black. What does this show?
options: The starch has been digested by the amylase
The sample now contains more starch than before
Protein has been broken down into amino acids
Fats have been emulsified by the amylase
questions.explain: Iodine turns blue-black only with starch, so a brown colour shows the starch has been broken down.

questions.q: In which region of the alimentary canal are most digested food molecules absorbed?
questions.explain: Most absorption of digested nutrients occurs across the wall of the small intestine.

questions.q: How are the villi lining the small intestine adapted for efficient absorption?
options: They have a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply
They have thick, muscular walls to grind food
They secrete acid to kill bacteria
They store bile until it is needed
questions.explain: A large surface area, a wall one cell thick and a rich blood supply all speed up the absorption of nutrients.

questions.q: The lining of the small intestine is folded and covered in millions of tiny villi. What is the main advantage of this structure?
options: It greatly increases the surface area for absorbing digested food
It slows food down so it can be stored
It increases the acidity needed for enzymes
It reduces the blood supply to the gut wall
questions.explain: The folds and villi provide a very large surface area, allowing more nutrients to be absorbed at once.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610) syllabus; Human Nutrition
